Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-[[:en:6th century|6th century]] during the late [[:en:Kofun period|Kofun period]]."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the [[:en:Shoku Nihongi|Shoku Nihongi]], as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-[[:en:6th century|6th century]] during the late [[:en:Kofun period|Kofun period]]."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-[[:en:6th century|6th century]] during the late [[:en:Kofun period|Kofun period]]."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the [[:en:Shoku Nihongi|Shoku Nihongi]], as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. Two individuals were interred. burial goods include iron swords, beads, and gold rings. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include swords, gold rings, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 4: Direct wooden coffin burial. == References == {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == {{small|(Sources used for this article)}} * Intypeational sign (Takaishi City, 1994) * {{Cite book|language=ja|year=1986|chapter=Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=458249028X|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Heibonsha)|1986}}}} * {{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kobayashi, Saburō|year=1989|chapter=Kurumazuka Kofun > Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}|publisher=Tokyo-do Publishing|isbn=4490102607|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Kofun)|1989}}}} == Related Articles == * [[:en:Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun]] * {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}} {{Kofun navbar}} {{translated page|ja|富木車塚古墳|version=93995667|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Zenpokoenfun]] [[Category:Completion tier 4]] }} [[ja:富木車塚古墳]] [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takaishi]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] [[Category:qq]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:qq]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:qq]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:qq]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:qq]][[Category:qq]] {{wikidata link|Q55530454}}

Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-[[:en:6th century|6th century]] during the late [[:en:Kofun period|Kofun period]]."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the [[:en:Shoku Nihongi|Shoku Nihongi]], as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-[[:en:6th century|6th century]] during the late [[:en:Kofun period|Kofun period]]."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]] with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No [[:en:Fukiishi|Fukiishi]] or [[:en:Haniwa|Haniwa]] were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]], were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-[[:en:6th century|6th century]] during the late [[:en:Kofun period|Kofun period]]."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the [[:en:Shoku Nihongi|Shoku Nihongi]], as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a {{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun}} with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No {{ill|Fukiishi|en|Fukiishi|WD=Q11621213|lt=Fukiishi}} or {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa}} were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-{{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century}} during the late {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}}."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi}}, as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. Two individuals were interred. burial goods include iron swords, beads, and gold rings. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include swords, gold rings, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 4: Direct wooden coffin burial. == References == {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == {{small|(Sources used for this article)}} * Intypeational sign (Takaishi City, 1994) * {{Cite book|language=ja|year=1986|chapter=Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=458249028X|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Heibonsha)|1986}}}} * {{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kobayashi, Saburō|year=1989|chapter=Kurumazuka Kofun > Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}|publisher=Tokyo-do Publishing|isbn=4490102607|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Kofun)|1989}}}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}} {{Kofun navbar}} {{translated page|ja|富木車塚古墳|version=93995667|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[ja:富木車塚古墳]] {{wikidata link|Q55530454}} [[Category:Completion tier 4]] [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takaishi]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Zenpokoenfun]]

The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a {{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun}} with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No {{ill|Fukiishi|en|Fukiishi|WD=Q11621213|lt=Fukiishi}} or {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa}} were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-{{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century}} during the late {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}}."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi}}, as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. Two individuals were interred. burial goods include iron swords, beads, and gold rings. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include swords, gold rings, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 4: Direct wooden coffin burial. == References == {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == {{small|(Sources used for this article)}} * Intypeational sign (Takaishi City, 1994) * {{Cite book|language=ja|year=1986|chapter=Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=458249028X|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Heibonsha)|1986}}}} * {{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kobayashi, Saburō|year=1989|chapter=Kurumazuka Kofun > Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}|publisher=Tokyo-do Publishing|isbn=4490102607|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Kofun)|1989}}}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}} {{Kofun navbar}} {{translated page|ja|富木車塚古墳|version=93995667|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[ja:富木車塚古墳]] {{wikidata link|Q55530454}} [[Category:Completion tier 4]] [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takaishi]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Zenpokoenfun]]

{| class="wikitable" style="background:#ffffff;text-align:center;font-size:85%;" |+Lineage of Izumi Northern Chief Tombs"Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. !part_of !Tomb name !type !area !built |- |North |{{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Kohanezuka Kofun}} |{{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun}} |94m |Late 4th century |- |South |Marukasa-yama Kofun |{{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun}} |96m |Late 4th century |- |South |Nabetsuka Kofun |{{ill|Round Kofun|ja|円墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Round Kofun|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} |60–70m |Early 5th century |- |South |Ōtsuka Kofun |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |46m |Mid-5th century |- |North |{{ill|Shinoda Kaibukiyama Kofun|ja|信太貝吹山古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinoda Kaibukiyama Kofun|qq=}} |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |60m |Early 5th century |- |North |Kaniya-zuka Kofun |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |Unknown |Late 5th century |- |North |'''Ōzono Kofun''' |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |50m |Late 5th century |- |North |{{ill|Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|ja|富木車塚古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|qq=}} |{{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun}} |48m |Mid-6th century |- |South |Kitsunezuka Kofun |{{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun}} |58m |Late 6th century |}
Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a {{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun}} with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No {{ill|Fukiishi|en|Fukiishi|WD=Q11621213|lt=Fukiishi}} or {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa}} were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-{{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century}} during the late {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}}."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi}}, as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. Two individuals were interred. burial goods include iron swords, beads, and gold rings. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include swords, gold rings, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 4: Direct wooden coffin burial. == References == {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == {{small|(Sources used for this article)}} * Intypeational sign (Takaishi City, 1994) * {{Cite book|language=ja|year=1986|chapter=Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=458249028X|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Heibonsha)|1986}}}} * {{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kobayashi, Saburō|year=1989|chapter=Kurumazuka Kofun > Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}|publisher=Tokyo-do Publishing|isbn=4490102607|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Kofun)|1989}}}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}} {{Kofun navbar}} {{translated page|ja|富木車塚古墳|version=93995667|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[ja:富木車塚古墳]] {{wikidata link|Q55530454}} [[Category:Completion tier 4]] [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takaishi]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Zenpokoenfun]] [[Category:pages]]

Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a {{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No {{ill|Fukiishi|en|Fukiishi|WD=Q11621213|lt=Fukiishi|1=Fukiishi}} or {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa|1=Haniwa}} were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery|1=Sue pottery}}, were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-{{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} during the late {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi|1=Shoku Nihongi}}, as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. Two individuals were interred. burial goods include iron swords, beads, and gold rings. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include swords, gold rings, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 4: Direct wooden coffin burial. == References == {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == {{small|(Sources used for this article)}} * Intypeational sign (Takaishi City, 1994) * {{Cite book|language=ja|year=1986|chapter=Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=458249028X|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Heibonsha)|1986}}}} * {{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kobayashi, Saburō|year=1989|chapter=Kurumazuka Kofun > Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}|publisher=Tokyo-do Publishing|isbn=4490102607|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Kofun)|1989}}}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|1=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}} {{Kofun navbar}} {{translated page|ja|富木車塚古墳|version=93995667|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[ja:富木車塚古墳]] {{wikidata link|Q55530454}} [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takaishi]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Zenpokoenfun]] [[Category:pages]]

The mound is no longer extant. == Overview ==
{| class="wikitable" style="background:#ffffff;text-align:center;font-size:85%;" |+Lineage of Izumi Northern Chief Tombs"Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. !part_of !Tomb name !type !area !built |- |North |{{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Kohanezuka Kofun|1=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} |{{ill|Zenpōkōenfun|en|Zenpōkōenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpōkōenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} |94m |Late 4th century |- |South |Marukasa-yama Kofun |{{ill|Zenpōkōenfun|en|Zenpōkōenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpōkōenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} |96m |Late 4th century |- |South |Nabetsuka Kofun |{{ill|Round Kofun|ja|円墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Round Kofun|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} |60–70m |Early 5th century |- |South |Ōtsuka Kofun |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |46m |Mid-5th century |- |North |{{ill|Shinoda Kaibukiyama Kofun|ja|信太貝吹山古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinoda Kaibukiyama Kofun|qq=}} |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |60m |Early 5th century |- |North |Kaniya-zuka Kofun |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |Unknown |Late 5th century |- |North |'''Ōzono Kofun''' |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |50m |Late 5th century |- |North |{{ill|Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|ja|富木車塚古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|qq=}} |{{ill|Zenpōkōenfun|en|Zenpōkōenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpōkōenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} |48m |Mid-6th century |- |South |Kitsunezuka Kofun |{{ill|Zenpōkōenfun|en|Zenpōkōenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpōkōenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} |58m |Late 6th century |}
Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a {{ill|Zenpōkōenfun|en|Zenpōkōenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpōkōenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}} with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No {{ill|Fukiishi|en|Fukiishi|WD=Q11621213|lt=Fukiishi|1=Fukiishi}} or {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa|1=Haniwa}} were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery|1=Sue pottery}}, were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-{{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} during the late {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi|1=Shoku Nihongi}}, as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. Two individuals were interred. burial goods include iron swords, beads, and gold rings. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include swords, gold rings, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 4: Direct wooden coffin burial. == References == {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == {{small|(Sources used for this article)}} * Intypeational sign (Takaishi City, 1994) * {{Cite book|language=ja|year=1986|chapter=Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=458249028X|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Heibonsha)|1986}}}} * {{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kobayashi, Saburō|year=1989|chapter=Kurumazuka Kofun > Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}|publisher=Tokyo-do Publishing|isbn=4490102607|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Kofun)|1989}}}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|1=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}} {{Kofun navbar}} {{translated page|ja|富木車塚古墳|version=93995667|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[ja:富木車塚古墳]] {{wikidata link|Q55530454}} [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takaishi]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Zenpōkōenfun]]

Intypeational sign at the site of Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun | alternate_name = | part_of = | location = {{ill|Takaishi, Osaka|en|Takaishi, Osaka|WD=Q857218|lt=Takaishi, Osaka|1=Takaishi, Osaka}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture|1=Osaka Prefecture}}, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34.522722|N|135.447853|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | type = {{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} | area = Mound length: 48m
Height: 5m (rear circular section) | burial = 7 burial facilities (including one {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}) | burial goods = Numerous burial goods | period = Mid {{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} | Historic Site = Not Historic Site1 | architectural_styles = {{ill|keyhole-shaped kofun|WD=Q11268718|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun|2=ja|3=前方後円墳|4=ko|5=전방후원분|6=zh|7=前方後圓墳}} }} '''Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun''' (富木車塚古墳) was a {{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} located in {{ill|Takaishi, Osaka|en|Takaishi, Osaka|WD=Q857218|lt=Takaishi, Osaka|1=Takaishi, Osaka}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture|1=Osaka Prefecture}}, Japan. The mound is no longer extant. == Overview ==
{| class="wikitable" style="background:#ffffff;text-align:center;font-size:85%;" |+Lineage of Izumi Northern Chief Tombs"Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. !part_of !Tomb name !type !area !built |- |North |{{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Kohanezuka Kofun|1=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} |{{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} |94m |Late 4th century |- |South |Marukasa-yama Kofun |{{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} |96m |Late 4th century |- |South |Nabetsuka Kofun |{{ill|Round Kofun|ja|円墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Round Kofun|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} |60–70m |Early 5th century |- |South |Ōtsuka Kofun |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |46m |Mid-5th century |- |North |{{ill|Shinoda Kaibukiyama Kofun|ja|信太貝吹山古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinoda Kaibukiyama Kofun|qq=}} |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |60m |Early 5th century |- |North |Kaniya-zuka Kofun |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |Unknown |Late 5th century |- |North |'''Ōzono Kofun''' |{{ill|scallop-shaped kofun|ja|帆立貝形古墳}} |50m |Late 5th century |- |North |{{ill|Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|ja|富木車塚古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|qq=}} |{{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} |48m |Mid-6th century |- |South |Kitsunezuka Kofun |{{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} |58m |Late 6th century |}
Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun was located on the northwestern terrace of the {{ill|Shinodayama Hills|ja|信太山丘陵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinodayama Hills|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 信太山演習場}} in southern Osaka. The site was excavated in 1959, but the mound was destroyed in the late 1960s due to residential development."Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. This destruction occurred despite the site having been archaeologically surveyed.Saitō, Kazuo. "The Problem of Kofun Destruction Due to Urban Development," in {{ill|Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja|日本建築学会論文報告集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Journal of Architectural Institute of Japan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Vol. 69, Architectural Institute of Japan, 1961. The tumulus was a {{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} with the front section oriented northwest.Kobayashi, Saburō. "Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun," in {{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}, Tokyo-do Publishing, 1989. No {{ill|Fukiishi|en|Fukiishi|WD=Q11621213|lt=Fukiishi|1=Fukiishi}} or {{ill|Haniwa|en|Haniwa|WD=Q849376|lt=Haniwa|1=Haniwa}} were found on the mound, and there was no evidence of a surrounding moat. The burial facilities included seven chambers containing the remains of 11 individuals along with various grave goods. Ritual ceramics, including large quantities of {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery|1=Sue pottery}}, were also recovered from the mound's neck section. The tumulus is believed to have been constructed in the mid-{{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} during the late {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}."Lineage of Izumi Northern Chiefs," in {{ill|Izumi City History Volume 6|ja|和泉の Municipal History6|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumi City History Volume 6|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Archaeology, Ancient, and Medieval, Izumi City Editorial Committee, Izumi City, Gyosei, 2013, pp. 65–70. It is considered significant for understanding family structures among powerful clans in the region at the time. The tomb has been linked to the {{ill|Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja|殿来氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki no Muraji clan|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi|1=Shoku Nihongi}}, as well as to the nearby {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}}."Takaishi City," in {{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume, Heibonsha, 1986. == Mound Specifications == The mound's estimated area are as follows: * Mound Length: 48 meters * Rear Circular Section ''' Diameter: 25 meters ''' Height: 5 meters * Front Section ''' Width: 18 meters ''' Height: 3 meters The mound was constructed entirely of piled earth. == burial == The burial facilities included seven separate chambers—three in the rear circular section (six individuals) and four in the front section (five individuals). Details are as follows: ; Rear Circular Section : These burials predate those in the front section. :* Chamber 1: {{ill|Yokoana-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, approximately 7m long and 1.2m wide, containing ceramic and wooden coffins. burial goods include gold rings, tubular beads, hollow silver beads, fragments of swords, and spears. :* Chamber 2: Clay coffin, measuring 1.94m by 0.8m. burial goods include iron swords, stone arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial, measuring 2.48m by 0.55m. burial goods include swords, wooden beads, and necklaces. ; Front Section : These burials occurred after those in the rear section. :* Chamber 1: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include antler hilt swords, iron arrowheads, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 2: Direct wooden coffin burial. Two individuals were interred. burial goods include iron swords, beads, and gold rings. :* Chamber 3: Direct wooden coffin burial. burial goods include swords, gold rings, and Sue pottery. :* Chamber 4: Direct wooden coffin burial. == References == {{Reflist}} == Bibliography == {{small|(Sources used for this article)}} * Intypeational sign (Takaishi City, 1994) * {{Cite book|language=ja|year=1986|chapter=Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Japanese Historical Topography Series|ja|日本歴史地名大系|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Historical Topography Series|qq=}} Osaka Volume|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=458249028X|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Heibonsha)|1986}}}} * {{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kobayashi, Saburō|year=1989|chapter=Kurumazuka Kofun > Tonoki Kurumazuka Kofun|title={{ill|Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|ja|日本古墳大辞典|1=Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Comprehensive Dictionary of Japanese Kofun|qq=}}|publisher=Tokyo-do Publishing|isbn=4490102607|ref={{Harvid|Tonoki Kofun (Kofun)|1989}}}} == Related Articles == * {{ill|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|en|Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|WD=Q11417846|lt=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun|1=Izumi Koganezuka Kofun}} * {{ill|Tonoki Shrine|ja|等乃伎神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tonoki Shrine|qq=}} {{Kofun navbar}} {{translated page|ja|富木車塚古墳|version=93995667|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{wikidata link|Q55530454|ja|富木車塚古墳}} [[Category:Kofun of Osaka prefecture]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takaishi]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Zenpō-kōen-fun]]
